claim: The Commander complex is a 16-subunit protein assembly that cooperates with other endosomal factors to recruit cargo proteins and facilitate the formation of tubulo-vesicular carriers.
source: A key player in endosomal recycling is the Commander complex, a 16-subunit protein assembly that cooperates with other endosomal factors to recruit cargo proteins and facilitate the formation of tubulo-vesicular carriers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to structural and functional studies of Commander throughout the manuscript.

claim: COMMD3 regulates a subset of cargo proteins independently of the other Commander subunits.
source: COMMD3 regulates a subset of cargo proteins independently of the other Commander subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative genetic analyses showing differential effects of COMMD3 vs. other COMMD protein knockouts on cargo trafficking (Figures 4, 5).

claim: The Commander-independent function of COMMD3 is mediated by its N-terminal domain (NTD).
source: The Commander-independent function of COMMD3 is mediated by its N-terminal domain (NTD), which binds and stabilizes ADP-ribosylation factor 1 (ARF1), a small GTPase regulating endosomal recycling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments showing that COMMD3-NTD alone can restore TfR surface levels in Commd3 KO cells (Figure 6B).

claim: COMMD3-NTD binds and stabilizes ARF1.
source: The Commander-independent function of COMMD3 is mediated by its N-terminal domain (NTD), which binds and stabilizes ADP-ribosylation factor 1 (ARF1), a small GTPase regulating endosomal recycling.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experiments (Figure 6G), co-localization studies (Figure 7A-B), and ARF1 stabilization assays (Figures 6G, 7C-D).

claim: Mutations disrupting the COMMD3-ARF1 interaction diminish ARF1 expression and impair COMMD3-dependent cargo recycling.
source: Mutations disrupting the COMMD3-ARF1 interaction diminish ARF1 expression and impair COMMD3-dependent cargo recycling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structure-guided mutagenesis experiments showing that COMMD3-NTD mutants fail to rescue TfR trafficking and ARF1 levels (Figure 8E-F).

claim: COMMD3 was the only Commander subunit isolated as a significant hit in a genome-wide CRISPR screen for GLUT-SPR surface homeostasis.
source: Genes encoding the unique subunits of the Retriever complex – Vps35l and Vps26c – were not isolated in the CRISPR screen (Figure 1C). Similarly, virtually none of the genes encoding the CCC complex were recovered as significant hits in the CRISPR screen, except for Commd3, which encodes the COMMD3 subunit of the Commander complex (Figure 1A–C; Healy et al., 2023).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C, which ranks genes from the CRISPR screen, with only Commd3 among Commander subunits appearing as a significant hit.

claim: The Commander complex is dispensable for the endosomal recycling of GLUT-SPR.
source: These data indicate that the Commander complex is dispensable for the endosomal recycling of GLUT-SPR.
evidence: This is inferred from the CRISPR screen results showing that genes encoding Retriever and CCC subunits (except Commd3) were not recovered as significant hits (Figure 1C).

claim: None of the genes encoding the Retromer and Commander complexes are essential for cell viability or growth in mouse preadipocytes.
source: We found that none of the genes encoding the Retromer and Commander complexes are essential in mouse preadipocytes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the essentiality screen data shown in Figure 1D, where none of these genes fall below the essentiality cutoff.

claim: Surface levels of GLUT-SPR were strongly reduced in Commd3 KO preadipocytes.
source: Indeed, surface levels of GLUT-SPR were strongly reduced in Commd3 KO preadipocytes, which were either cultured under standard conditions or stimulated with insulin to mimic a physiological fed state (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 2B comparing WT and Commd3 KO cells.

claim: Surface GLUT-SPR levels were markedly reduced in Commd3 KO adipocytes.
source: Using flow cytometry, we observed that surface GLUT-SPR levels were markedly reduced in Commd3 KO adipocytes (Figure 2C), indicating that the role of COMMD3 in surface protein homeostasis is not restricted to a single cell type.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 2C and confocal imaging in Figure 2D.

claim: The morphology of EEA1-positive endosomes was significantly altered in Commd3 KO cells.
source: We observed that the morphology of EEA1-positive endosomes was significantly altered in Commd3 KO cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by confocal imaging in Figure 3A and quantification in Figure 3B showing increased endosome size.

claim: The size of the EEA1-positive endosomes markedly increased in Commd3 KO cells.
source: The size of the EEA1-positive endosomes markedly increased in Commd3 KO cells (Figure 3A and B), reminiscent of the endosome enlargement observed in Retromer-deficient cells (Neuman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 3B showing increased EEA1-positive puncta area in KO cells.

claim: GLUT-SPR accumulation in EEA1-positive endosomes was elevated in Commd3 KO cells.
source: We also observed elevated GLUT-SPR accumulation in EEA1-positive endosomes in Commd3 KO cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 3C showing increased GFP mean fluorescence intensity in EEA1-positive puncta.

claim: Co-localization of GLUT-SPR with Rab5 increased in Commd3 KO cells.
source: We found that a portion of GLUT-SPR resided in Rab5-positive compartments and its co-localization with Rab5 increased in Commd3 KO cells (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is shown by SIM imaging in Figure 3D and quantified in Figure 3E.

claim: Surface levels of ITGA6 were downregulated in Commd1, Commd3, and Commd5 KO cell lines.
source: As expected, surface levels of ITGA6 were downregulated in all these KO cell lines (Figure 4A), confirming the canonical role of COMMD3 within the Commander holo-complex.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 4A comparing WT with Commd1, Commd3, and Commd5 KO cells.

claim: Surface levels of GLUT-SPR were slightly increased in Commd1 KO cells, in contrast to the strong reduction observed in Commd3 KO cells.
source: We found that surface levels of GLUT-SPR were slightly increased in the Commd1 KO cells, in contrast to the strong reduction observed in Commd3 KO cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 4B comparing different COMMD KO cell lines.

claim: Surface levels of TfR were markedly decreased in Commd3 KO cells but remained intact in Commd1 or Commd5 KO populations.
source: Surface levels of the transferrin receptor (TfR), a Commander-independent cargo (Puthenveedu et al., 2010), were markedly decreased in Commd3 KO cells but remained intact in Commd1 or Commd5 KO populations (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 4C showing differential effects of COMMD protein knockouts on TfR surface levels.

claim: Total TfR levels decreased in Commd3 KO cells.
source: Total TfR levels also decreased in Commd3 KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), consistent with the notion that unretrieved cargo is routed to the lysosome for degradation (Healy et al., 2023; Simonetti and Cullen, 2019; Cullen and Steinberg, 2018).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and is consistent with known mechanisms of cargo degradation.

claim: Surface levels of LAMP1 were strongly decreased in Commd3 KO cells but were not substantially changed in Commd1 or Commd5 KO cells.
source: Surface levels of lysosomal-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) were also strongly decreased in Commd3 KO cells but were not substantially changed in Commd1 or Commd5 KO cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 4D comparing different COMMD KO cell lines.

claim: COMMD3 expression was upregulated in Ccdc93 or Vps35l KO cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed that COMMD3 expression was not reduced but upregulated in Ccdc93 or Vps35l KO cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 5A and quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Surface levels of TfR were markedly increased in Ccdc93 or Vps35l KO cells.
source: Indeed, we observed that surface levels of TfR, a cargo dependent on Commd3 but not on the Commander complex (Figure 4C; Puthenveedu et al., 2010), were markedly increased in Ccdc93 or Vps35l KO cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 5B showing elevated TfR surface levels in these KO cells.

claim: Expression of the COMMD3 NTD fully restored the surface levels of TfR in Commd3 KO cells while the CTD did not.
source: Indeed, expression of the COMMD3 NTD fully restored the surface levels of TfR in Commd3 KO cells while the CTD did not (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that the NTD is sufficient for this function.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 6B comparing rescue with NTD vs. CTD constructs.

claim: ARF1 emerged as a strong candidate interactor of COMMD3-NTD from proteomic analysis.
source: Among these proteins, ARF1 emerged as a strong candidate because it acts as a membrane trafficking regulator known to function on endosomes (Figure 6F; Nakai et al., 2013; Stockhammer et al., 2024).
evidence: This is shown in the proteomic data scatter plot in Figure 6F and supported by citations to ARF1's known functions.

claim: The NTD of COMMD3 interacted with ARF1 in co-IP experiments.
source: Using co-IP, we observed that the NTD of COMMD3 interacted with ARF1 (Figure 6G), confirming the results of the proteomic experiments.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP immunoblots in Figure 6G showing ARF1 binding to COMMD3-NTD.

claim: Significant co-localization was observed between ARF1 and the NTD of COMMD3.
source: We observed significant co-localization between ARF1 and the NTD of COMMD3 (Figure 7A and B), consistent with their interactions detected in proteomic and co-IP experiments (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown by SIM imaging in Figure 7A and quantified in Figure 7B showing high Pearson correlation coefficient.

claim: ARF1 expression levels were significantly elevated when co-expressed with the NTD of COMMD3.
source: We noted that, in the co-IP assays using 293T cells, ARF1 expression levels were significantly elevated when co-expressed with the NTD of COMMD3 (Figure 6G). A similar ARF1-stabilizing effect was also observed in HeLa cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figures 6G and 7C demonstrating increased ARF1 protein levels in the presence of COMMD3-NTD.

claim: ARF1 levels were markedly reduced in Commd3 KO cells and were fully restored upon introduction of a COMMD3 rescue gene.
source: Interestingly, we found that ARF1 levels were markedly reduced in Commd3 KO cells and were fully restored upon introduction of a COMMD3 rescue gene (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data in Figure 7D comparing ARF1 levels in WT, KO, and rescue cell lines.

claim: ARF1 overexpression fully restored the surface levels of TfR in Commd3 KO cells.
source: Strikingly, ARF1 overexpression fully restored the surface levels of TfR in Commd3 KO cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 7E demonstrating rescue of TfR surface levels by ARF1 overexpression.

claim: AlphaFold3 predicted a high-confidence structure of the ARF1-GTP:COMMD3-NTD heterodimeric complex.
source: AlphaFold3 predicted a high-confidence structure of the ARF1-GTP:COMMD3-NTD heterodimeric complex (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A displaying the predicted structural model with confidence scores.

claim: The α1 helix of COMMD3-NTD binds to the switch 1 of ARF1, while the α3 and α4 helices of COMMD3-NTD interact with the switch 2 of ARF1.
source: According to this structural model, the α1 helix of COMMD3-NTD binds to the switch 1 of ARF1, while the α3 and α4 helices of COMMD3-NTD interact with the switch 2 of ARF1 (Figure 8A and B, Source data 1).
evidence: This is based on the AlphaFold3 structural prediction shown in Figure 8A with detailed interface analysis.

claim: The binding of COMMD3 to ARF1 is mainly mediated by hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds.
source: The binding of COMMD3 to ARF1 is mainly mediated by hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds, including hydrogen bonds formed by K60 and H61 of COMMD3 with Y81 of ARF1, K60 of COMMD3 with R79 and Q83 of ARF1, H63 of COMMD3 with H80 of ARF1 (Figure 8A and B, Source data 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the AlphaFold3 model shown in Figure 8A.

claim: COMMD3 selectively recognizes the GTP-bound form of ARF1.
source: AphaFold3 did not predict high-confidence structural models between COMMD3-NTD and ARF1-GDP or apo-ARF1, suggesting that COMMD3 selectively recognizes the GTP-bound form of ARF1.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability of AlphaFold3 to predict high-confidence models with ARF1-GDP or apo-ARF1, and is consistent with stabilization of GTP-bound ARF1 shown in Figures 6G and 7C.

claim: The COMMD3-NTD mutant failed to restore surface levels of TfR in Commd3 KO cells.
source: We observed that the COMMD3-NTD mutant failed to restore surface levels of TfR, whereas WT COMMD3-NTD fully rescued the KO phenotype (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8E comparing rescue with WT vs. mutant COMMD3-NTD.

claim: WT COMMD3-NTD, but not the mutant, restored ARF1 expression in Commd3 KO cells.
source: In agreement with this finding, WT COMMD3-NTD, but not the mutant, restored ARF1 expression in Commd3 KO cells (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot quantification in Figure 8F comparing ARF1 levels with WT vs. mutant COMMD3-NTD rescue.

claim: Deletion of Commd3 leads to the enlargement of early endosomes and accumulation of GLUT-SPR in these compartments.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that deletion of Commd3 leads to the enlargement of early endosomes and accumulation of GLUT-SPR in these compartments, consistent with a trafficking defect occurring at the endosomal recycling step.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging and quantification in Figure 3 showing enlarged EEA1-positive endosomes and increased GLUT-SPR accumulation.

claim: COMMD3 regulates endosomal trafficking through binding and stabilizing ARF1.
source: These data demonstrate that COMMD3 regulates endosomal trafficking through binding and stabilizing ARF1.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence including co-IP (Figure 6G), co-localization (Figure 7A-B), stabilization assays (Figures 6G, 7C-D), and rescue experiments (Figure 7E).

claim: The Commander complex primarily sorts cargoes from endosomal compartments to the plasma membrane.
source: The Commander complex, which primarily sorts cargoes from endosomal compartments to the plasma membrane, is a large protein complex composed of the Retriever subcomplex and the CCC subcomplex (COMMD-CCDC22-CCDC93) (Figure 1A; Healy et al., 2023; Boesch et al., 2024; Yong et al., 2023; Laulumaa et al., 2024; Leneva and Kovtun, 2024; Mallam and Marcotte, 2017; McNally et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to Commander studies.

claim: The Retriever subcomplex is a heterotrimer consisting of VPS35L/C16ORF62, VPS26C/DSCR3, and VPS29.
source: The Retriever subcomplex is a heterotrimer consisting of VPS35L/C16ORF62, VPS26C/DSCR3, and VPS29 and shares a similar overall configuration with Retromer (McNally et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to McNally et al., 2017.

claim: The CCC complex includes 10 COMMD proteins (COMMD1-10).
source: The CCC complex includes 10 COMMD proteins (COMMD1-10), which interact through their conserved C-terminal copper metabolism MURR1 domains (COMMDs) (Singla et al., 2019; van De Sluis et al., 2002; Burstein et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The COMMD proteins bind CCDC22 and CCDC93 to form the CCC subcomplex, which also contains DENND10.
source: The COMMD proteins bind CCDC22 and CCDC93 to form the CCC subcomplex, which also contains DENND10 (Healy et al., 2023; Leneva and Kovtun, 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to recent structural studies.

claim: The 13-subunit CCC subcomplex combines with the Retriever subcomplex to form the 16-subunit Commander holo-complex.
source: The 13-subunit CCC subcomplex combines with the Retriever subcomplex to form the 16-subunit Commander holo-complex (Figure 1A; Healy et al., 2023; Boesch et al., 2024; Laulumaa et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A, supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Retromer is a heterotrimeric complex comprised of VPS35, VPS29, and VPS26.
source: Retromer, a heterotrimeric complex comprised of VPS35, VPS29, and VPS26, recruits cargo proteins on the endosome and mediates the formation of tubulo-vesicular carriers for retrograde trafficking to the TGN or recycling to the plasma membrane (Wang et al., 2018; Rothman and Stevens, 1986; Bankaitis et al., 1986; Seaman et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to foundational Retromer studies.

claim: The GLUT-SPR-based CRISPR screen isolated Vps35 and Vps29.
source: The GLUT-SPR-based CRISPR screen isolated Vps35 and Vps29 (Figure 1C), which encode subunits of the Retromer complex, consistent with the critical role of Retromer in the endosomal recycling of GLUT4 (Gulbranson et al., 2017; Pan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with known functions of Retromer in GLUT4 trafficking.

claim: Genes encoding Vps26 were not recovered in the screen due to redundancy (Vps26a and Vps26b).
source: Genes encoding Vps26 were not recovered in the screen due to redundancy (Vps26a and Vps26b).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why Vps26 genes were not isolated despite Retromer's role in GLUT-SPR trafficking.

claim: The CRISPR screen has the sensitivity and specificity to systematically examine the functional roles of endosomal recycling genes.
source: Recovery of the Retromer genes also suggests that the CRISPR screen has the sensitivity and specificity to systematically examine the functional roles of endosomal recycling genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful recovery of known Retromer genes (Vps35, Vps29) in the screen.

claim: The disruption of either the Retromer or Commander-dependent endosomal retrieval pathways does not impair the viability or proliferation of mouse preadipocytes.
source: Thus, the disruption of either the Retromer or Commander-dependent endosomal retrieval pathways does not impair the viability or proliferation of these cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the essentiality screen data in Figure 1D showing that none of these genes are essential.

claim: COMMD3 plays an unrecognized role in GLUT-SPR trafficking, independent of its canonical function within the Commander holo-complex.
source: Together, these global genetic analyses suggest that COMMD3 plays an unrecognized role in GLUT-SPR trafficking, independent of its canonical function within the Commander holo-complex.
evidence: This is concluded from the CRISPR screen results showing Commd3 as the only Commander subunit recovered as a significant hit.

claim: The role of COMMD3 in surface protein homeostasis is not restricted to a single cell type.
source: Using flow cytometry, we observed that surface GLUT-SPR levels were markedly reduced in Commd3 KO adipocytes (Figure 2C), indicating that the role of COMMD3 in surface protein homeostasis is not restricted to a single cell type.
evidence: This is demonstrated by showing COMMD3's effects in both preadipocytes and differentiated adipocytes (Figures 2B-D).

claim: COMMD3 has a critical role in the endosomal trafficking of GLUT-SPR.
source: These results demonstrated a critical role of COMMD3 in the endosomal trafficking of GLUT-SPR.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple experiments showing reduced surface GLUT-SPR levels and altered endosomal morphology in Commd3 KO cells (Figures 2-3).

claim: Comparative analysis demonstrates that COMMD3 regulates a group of cargo proteins independent of the Commander holo-complex, in addition to its canonical function within the Commander complex.
source: Together, comparative analysis of these diverse membrane proteins clearly demonstrates that COMMD3 regulates a group of cargo proteins independent of the Commander holo-complex, in addition to its canonical function within the Commander complex.
evidence: This is concluded from comparative KO experiments showing differential effects on ITGA6 (Commander-dependent) vs. TfR and LAMP1 (COMMD3-dependent but Commander-independent) (Figure 4).

claim: COMMD3 expression was substantially decreased in Commd3 KO cells.
source: Representative immunoblots showing the indicated proteins in wild-type (WT) and Commd3 KO mouse preadipocytes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A immunoblot where COMMD3 band is absent in KO cells.

claim: The expression of CCDC93 and VPS35L was substantially decreased in Commd3 KO cells.
source: We observed that the expression of CCDC93 and VPS35L was substantially decreased in Commd3 KO cells, and VPS35L expression was diminished in Ccdc93 KO cells.
evidence: This is shown in immunoblots in Figure 5A demonstrating interdependent stability of Commander subunits.

claim: VPS35L expression was diminished in Ccdc93 KO cells.
source: We observed that the expression of CCDC93 and VPS35L was substantially decreased in Commd3 KO cells, and VPS35L expression was diminished in Ccdc93 KO cells.
evidence: This is shown in immunoblots in Figure 5A.

claim: Stability of subunits within a protein complex is interdependent.
source: These findings are consistent with the notion that stability of subunits within a protein complex is interdependent (Wang et al., 2023; Gulbranson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the observed co-dependent stability of Commander subunits, supported by citations.

claim: COMMD3 persists when other subunits of the Commander complex are depleted.
source: Thus, unlike other Commander subunits, COMMD3 persists when other subunits of the Commander complex are depleted, further supporting the ability of COMMD3 to regulate endosomal trafficking independent of the Commander holo-complex.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that COMMD3 is upregulated rather than degraded in Ccdc93 or Vps35l KO cells (Figure 5A).

claim: The upregulation of COMMD3 in Commander-deficient cells likely reflects a compensatory mechanism.
source: The upregulation of COMMD3 in Commander-deficient cells, which likely reflects a compensatory mechanism, offers another strategy to test the Commander-independent function of COMMD3.
evidence: This is proposed as a speculative explanation for the observed COMMD3 upregulation.

claim: TfR is a cargo dependent on Commd3 but not on the Commander complex.
source: We reasoned that if a cargo is dependent on COMMD3 but not on the Commander complex, its surface levels could be increased in cells with elevated COMMD3. Indeed, we observed that surface levels of TfR, a cargo dependent on Commd3 but not on the Commander complex (Figure 4C; Puthenveedu et al., 2010), were markedly increased in Ccdc93 or Vps35l KO cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing TfR surface levels across different KO cell lines (Figures 4C, 5B) and supported by citation to Puthenveedu et al., 2010.

claim: Surface TfR levels were diminished in Commd3 KO cells and were fully restored by expression of a Commd3 rescue gene.
source: Conversely, surface TfR levels were diminished in Commd3 KO cells and were fully restored by expression of a Commd3 rescue gene (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 5B demonstrating rescue of the KO phenotype.

claim: KO of both Commd3 and Ccdc93 resulted in decreased surface levels of TfR.
source: KO of both Commd3 and Ccdc93 resulted in decreased surface levels of TfR (Figure 5C), confirming that the elevated surface TfR observed in Ccdc93 KO cells was caused by COMMD3 upregulation.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 5C comparing double KO with single KO cells.

claim: Overexpression of Commd3 in WT cells markedly elevated TfR surface levels.
source: Consistent with this notion, overexpression of Commd3 in WT cells markedly elevated TfR surface levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 5D demonstrating gain-of-function effects.

claim: COMMD3 is upregulated in Retriever- or CCDC93-deficient cells and enhances the endosomal retrieval of COMMD3-dependent cargoes.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that COMMD3 is upregulated in Retriever- or CCDC93-deficient cells and enhances the endosomal retrieval of COMMD3-dependent cargoes, further supporting a Commander-independent role of COMMD3 in endosomal recycling.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments showing COMMD3 upregulation and increased TfR surface levels in Ccdc93 or Vps35l KO cells (Figure 5).

claim: The COMMD3 protein is comprised of two autonomously folded domains – NTD and CTD.
source: The COMMD3 protein is comprised of two autonomously folded domains – NTD and CTD (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 6A showing the domain structure.

claim: The C-terminal COMMD domains of COMMD proteins are well-conserved and mediate the formation of the heterodecameric COMMD complex within the Commander holo-complex.
source: The C-terminal COMMD domains of COMMD proteins are well-conserved and mediate the formation of the heterodecameric COMMD complex within the Commander holo-complex (Boesch et al., 2024; Maine and Burstein, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The NTDs of COMMD proteins share a similar structure but are more divergent in sequence.
source: The NTDs of COMMD proteins share a similar structure but are more divergent in sequence (Laulumaa et al., 2024; Healy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The function of the COMMD NTDs is unknown.
source: The function of the COMMD NTDs is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The NTD of COMMD3 is sufficient for its Commander-independent function.
source: Indeed, expression of the COMMD3 NTD fully restored the surface levels of TfR in Commd3 KO cells while the CTD did not (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that the NTD is sufficient for this function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments in Figure 6B showing that NTD alone can restore TfR surface levels.

claim: ARF1 acts as a membrane trafficking regulator known to function on endosomes.
source: Among these proteins, ARF1 emerged as a strong candidate because it acts as a membrane trafficking regulator known to function on endosomes (Figure 6F; Nakai et al., 2013; Stockhammer et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to ARF1 studies.

claim: The ARF family of proteins is small GTPases involved in the recruitment of coat proteins, activation of membrane lipid-modifying enzymes, and interaction with the cytoskeleton.
source: The ARF family of proteins is small GTPases involved in the recruitment of coat proteins, activation of membrane lipid-modifying enzymes, and interaction with the cytoskeleton (Stockhammer et al., 2024; D'Souza-Schorey and Chavrier, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The switches 1 and 2 of ARF1 are highly conserved regions that are regulated by GTP binding and interact with effectors involved in endosomal recycling.
source: The switches 1 and 2 of ARF1 are highly conserved regions that are regulated by GTP binding and interact with effectors involved in endosomal recycling (Goldberg, 1998; Sauvageau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations to ARF1 studies.

claim: COMMD3 strongly stabilizes GTP-bound ARF1.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the observation that COMMD3 strongly stabilizes GTP-bound ARF1 (Figures 6G and 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing increased ARF1 levels when co-expressed with COMMD3-NTD (Figures 6G, 7C).

claim: GTP-ARF1 is intrinsically unstable prior to engaging its effectors and requires stabilization by COMMD3.
source: These findings suggest that GTP-ARF1 is intrinsically unstable prior to engaging its effectors and, therefore, requires stabilization by COMMD3.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the ARF1 stabilization data.

claim: COMMD3 must dissociate from ARF1 before the latter can engage its effectors to regulate endosomal recycling.
source: Since COMMD3 binds to the same regions of ARF1 recognized by ARF1 effectors, it must dissociate from ARF1 before the latter can engage its effectors to regulate endosomal recycling (Stockhammer et al., 2024).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model showing COMMD3 binding to ARF1 switch regions that are also recognized by effectors.

claim: COMMD proteins are known to exist outside the Commander holo-complex.
source: COMMD proteins are known to exist outside the Commander holo-complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: COMMD proteins can form homo- or hetero-oligomers independently of other Commander subunits.
source: While they are unstable as monomers, COMMD proteins can form homo- or hetero-oligomers independently of other Commander subunits (Healy et al., 2018; Shirai et al., 2023; Nakai et al., 2019; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: COMMD3 likely forms homo-oligomers before associating with ARF1 to regulate cargo trafficking in a Commander-independent manner.
source: Since other COMMD proteins were not identified as significant hits in our GLUT-SPR-based CRISPR screen, COMMD3 likely forms homo-oligomers before associating with ARF1 to regulate cargo trafficking in a Commander-independent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the CRISPR screen results showing only Commd3 as a hit, combined with knowledge that COMMD proteins can form oligomers.

claim: The Commander-independent function of COMMD3 offers an additional route of endosomal recycling, alongside the Retromer- and Commander-dependent recycling pathways.
source: The Commander-independent function of COMMD3 offers an additional route of endosomal recycling, alongside the Retromer- and Commander-dependent recycling pathways.
evidence: This is proposed as an interpretation of the findings in the discussion.

claim: By leveraging existing proteins such as COMMD3, the cell expands the repertoire of endosomal recycling routes without increasing gene numbers.
source: By leveraging existing proteins such as COMMD3, the cell expands the repertoire of endosomal recycling routes without increasing gene numbers, which helps meet the formidable challenge of sorting thousands of membrane proteins that are constantly endocytosed into the cell.
evidence: This is proposed as a speculative interpretation of the biological significance of the findings.

claim: Other COMMD proteins may also possess additional functions outside the Commander holo-complex.
source: Our findings raise the intriguing possibility that other COMMD proteins may also possess additional functions outside the Commander holo-complex.
evidence: This is proposed as a speculative extension of the findings.

claim: Commander is implicated in biological pathways including vesicle fusion, cytoskeletal organization, intracellular signaling, protein degradation, and gene expression.
source: In addition to endosomal recycling, Commander is also implicated in biological pathways including vesicle fusion, cytoskeletal organization, intracellular signaling, protein degradation, and gene expression (Ambrosio et al., 2022; McNally et al., 2017; Singla et al., 2019; Shirai et al., 2023; Nakai et al., 2019; Campion et al., 2018; Suraweera et al., 2021; Li et al., 2015; Bartuzi et al., 2013; Esposito et al., 2016; O'Hara et al., 2014; Riera‐Romo, 2018; You et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2011; de Bie et al., 2006; Maine et al., 2007; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Bartuzi et al., 2016; Hancock et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2013; Weiskirchen and Penning, 2021; Jiang et al., 2019; Dumoulin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by extensive citations.

claim: Commander subunits exhibit distinct tissue-specific expression patterns.

claim: The Commander complex's 16 subunits display a stringent equimolar stoichiometry within the holo-complex.
